ta-l3d23q3-d1e108.summary: Prooemium to the third question of Distinction 23, on the formation of faith. It lists four articles: whether faith is formed by charity, whether unformed faith is a gift of God, whether it exists in demons, and whether it remains when charity comes.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e125.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 1 (is faith formed by charity?): form must precede, being the principle of the thing, but charity is posterior to faith. So charity does not form faith.
claims: Since form precedes and charity follows faith, charity cannot be faith's form.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e128.summary: Second objection: everything has its species from its own form, and faith differs in species from charity. So charity is not faith's form.
claims: A form gives species, and faith and charity differ in species.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e131.summary: Third objection: one thing does not have several forms, and faith is formed by grace. So it is not formed by charity.
claims: Faith, formed by grace, cannot also be formed by charity.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e134.summary: Sed contra: without charity faith cannot elicit the meritorious act it elicits when charity comes, so charity gives faith some power and in some way forms it.
claims: Charity enables faith's meritorious act and so in some way forms faith.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e138.summary: Second sed contra: a thing's form is its beauty, and faith becomes beautiful and acceptable to God through charity.
claims: Charity makes faith acceptable to God and so is its form.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e147.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 2 (is unformed faith a virtue?): Augustine says the virtues other than charity can be in good and bad people alike, so faith as a virtue can be in the wicked, and that faith is unformed.
claims: Augustine allows virtues other than charity in the wicked, so unformed faith is a virtue.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e150.summary: Second objection: virtue concerns the difficult and is praised for it, and believing the articles is most difficult; the praise of faith is to believe what one does not see. So unformed faith, which believes all the articles, is a virtue.
claims: Unformed faith accomplishes the difficult and praiseworthy act of believing the articles, so it is a virtue.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e156.summary: Third objection: only a virtue or a vice is opposed to a vice. Unformed faith is opposed to the vice of unbelief and is not a vice, so it is a virtue.
claims: Unformed faith, as the opposite of unbelief, must be a virtue.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e159.summary: Sed contra: unformed faith is dead (James), and nothing dead has the ratio of virtue.
claims: Dead faith cannot be a virtue.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e163.summary: Second sed contra: no one uses virtue badly (Augustine), but one can use unformed faith badly.
claims: Since unformed faith can be misused, it is not a virtue.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e172.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 3 (do formed and unformed faith differ in species?): what differs in genus differs in species, and formed faith is a virtue while unformed is not. So they differ in species.
claims: Formed and unformed faith differ in genus and hence in species.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e175.summary: Second objection: species comes from form, and charity is faith's form. So unformed faith is not of the same species as formed.
claims: Lacking its form, unformed faith lacks the species of formed faith.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e178.summary: Third objection: the same specific form has the same specific act. The act of formed faith is believing in God, which unformed faith lacks. So they differ in species.
claims: Different acts indicate different species of faith.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e181.summary: Sed contra: habits are diversified by acts and objects, and formed and unformed faith have the same proper object, the one truth. So they do not differ in species.
claims: Sharing one object, formed and unformed faith are of one species.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e185.summary: Second sed contra: what is outside a thing's essence does not change its species, as light coming to the air. Charity is a habit essentially separate from faith, so formed faith does not differ in species from unformed.
claims: Charity, extrinsic to faith's essence, does not change its species.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e195.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 1. In ordered agents the ends of secondary agents are ordered to the end of the first, as an army to its general's good. So the first agent's action is both prior and posterior: prior in moving, since one command grounds all the others' actions and is specified in each, as one soldier takes a sword and another readies a horse; posterior in using the others' acts for its own end. Among the soul's powers the will is first mover, commanding the other powers' acts for the last end and using them to attain it. So the powers moved by the will receive two things from it. First, a form impressed by the mover: either from the will's own form (they share its freedom) or from the habit perfecting the will, charity, so that all habits in powers moved by a perfect will participate in the form of charity. This form is common to all, and each habit also has a special form proper to its power and object. Second, they receive their consummation in the end, and in this way charity is called the end of the other virtues, uniting them to the last end. Since faith is in the intellect as moved by the will, charity forms it with this common form, while faith keeps its special form from its own object and power, and receives its consummation through charity.
claims: In ordered agents the first agent's action is prior in moving and posterior in using the others' acts.
The will, as first mover among the soul's powers, impresses its form on the powers it moves and brings them to the end.
Charity, perfecting the will, is a common form participated by all habits in powers moved by the will, while each habit keeps its own special form.
Charity forms faith with this common form and consummates it in the end, while faith keeps its specific form from its object and subject.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e198.summary: Reply to the first objection: faith simply precedes charity, since the willing faith requires can exist without charity; but formed faith follows charity.
claims: Faith as such precedes charity, while formed faith follows it.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e201.summary: Reply to the second objection: all virtues agree in their end, so their acts do not differ by the mode charity gives them through ordering to the end, but by the mode they have from their power and proper object. By that form faith is distinguished from charity and is not formed by it.
claims: Faith's specific form comes from its power and object, not from charity, which supplies only the common form of ordering to the end.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e204.summary: Reply to the third objection: faith is formed by grace through the mediation of charity, since the act of faith is acceptable to God insofar as it proceeds from charity.
claims: Grace forms faith through charity.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e213.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 2: virtue produces a perfect act, and the act of a power moved by another is perfect only if both are perfected by habits, the superior so as not to fail in directing or moving and the inferior so as not to fail in executing. For example, a temperate act requires temperance in the concupiscible and prudence in reason; without prudence any disposition of the concupiscible lacks the ratio of virtue. Believing is an act of the intellect moved by the will, so for it to be perfect the intellect must be perfected by the light of faith and the will by charity. Unformed faith lacks a perfect act and is therefore not a virtue.
claims: An act of a moved power is perfect only when both mover and moved are perfected by habits.
Believing requires both the light of faith in the intellect and charity in the will to be perfect.
Unformed faith, lacking charity, does not produce a perfect act and so is not a virtue.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e216.summary: Reply to the first objection: Augustine uses 'virtue' broadly for any disposition inclining to an act in which good is done.
claims: Augustine's usage of 'virtue' there is broad.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e219.summary: Reply to the second objection: virtue requires not only doing what virtue does but doing it as the virtuous person does, though one may be praised somewhat for doing virtuous things. That mode is missing in the act of unformed faith, so it is not a virtue.
claims: Virtue requires the virtuous mode of acting, which unformed faith lacks.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e222.summary: Reply to the third objection: a disposition to virtue is also opposed to vice, so unformed faith need not be a virtue to oppose unbelief.
claims: Dispositions to virtue also oppose vice.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e231.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 3: habits differ according to their acts, which can be considered by their natural species or their moral species. These can diverge: killing a guilty and an innocent person are the same natural species but different moral species, while executing a robber and freeing an innocent are different natural species but the same moral species (justice). By natural species, taken from the proper object, the acts of formed and unformed faith are the same. By moral species they differ as complete and incomplete within the same species, like doing just things not as the just person does and as the just person does. So formed and unformed faith are wholly the same in natural species and differ morally only as perfect and imperfect in one species, like disposition and habit of virtue.
claims: Acts can be considered by natural species (from object) or moral species, and these can diverge.
Formed and unformed faith are the same in natural species.
In moral species they differ only as perfect and imperfect within one species, not as distinct species.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e234.summary: Reply to the first objection: virtue is the genus of faith in the moral order, and unformed faith is not wholly foreign to it but is imperfect within that genus.
claims: Unformed faith is an imperfect member of the moral genus of virtue.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e237.summary: Reply to the second objection: virtue has its natural species from the form it has through its power and proper object, and its moral species from the form it has from the moving and directing power. So they do not differ in species except as stated.
claims: Natural species comes from power and object, moral species from the moving power.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e240.summary: Reply to the third objection: as said earlier, the three formulas designate one numerical act under different aspects. So something is in the act of formed faith that is not in unformed faith, but it is not wholly another act.
claims: Formed faith's act adds something to unformed faith's act without being a wholly different act.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e253.summary: First objection: Augustine says faith is acquired, nourished and defended by knowledge, and no habit acquired by knowledge is an infused gift of God. So unformed faith is not infused.
claims: Faith acquired through knowledge is an acquired habit.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e259.summary: Second objection: faith comes from hearing (Romans 10), Thomas believed because he saw (John 20:29), a gloss reads 'call your husband' as 'call the intellect to believe', and no one believes unless willing. So faith comes from something in us and is therefore acquired.
claims: Faith arises from hearing, seeing, intellect and will, all of which are in us, so it is acquired.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e281.summary: Third objection: the philosophers believed God omnipotent without any infused habit.
claims: Philosophers believed in divine omnipotence without infused faith.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e285.summary: Fourth objection: a habit suffices of itself to move its power to act, but the believer cannot perform the act of faith without instruction. So faith is acquired.
claims: Faith's dependence on instruction shows it is acquired.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e288.summary: Fifth objection: God's works are perfect (Deuteronomy 32:4), but unformed faith is imperfect. So it is not from God.
claims: Unformed faith's imperfection shows it is not from God.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e299.summary: Sixth objection: the act of sin is not said to be from God because of its attached deformity. Unformed faith has a deformity, so it is not from God.
claims: Like sin, unformed faith's deformity excludes it from divine causation.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e302.summary: Sed contra: a gloss on 1 Corinthians 13:2 says faith without charity is a gift of God, since many gifts of God are in the wicked. So unformed faith is infused.
claims: Faith without charity is a gift of God.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e313.summary: Second sed contra: no one can do what is above nature except by something divinely given, and one with unformed faith assents to what is above nature.
claims: Assent to the supernatural requires a divinely infused principle.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e316.summary: Third sed contra: the matters of faith are higher than those of prophecy, and prophecy requires infused light in the wicked as in the good. So much more does faith.
claims: If prophecy requires infused light even in the wicked, so does faith.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e320.summary: Aquinas's determination: habits are needed to determine powers not naturally determined to perfect acts. Sometimes a lower power is not so determined but a higher one is, as reason is naturally determined to the mean in pleasures, so temperance is acquired in the concupiscible by the force of reason. But no power is naturally determined to what exceeds reason, which is faith's matter. So for this act we need a habit that is not acquired. Infused faith helps in two ways: it makes the intellect ready to believe what is to be believed, against hardness, and discerning in rejecting what is not to be believed, against error.
claims: Acquired habits arise when a higher power is naturally determined to what the lower lacks.
No power is naturally determined to what exceeds reason, so the habit of faith cannot be acquired.
Infused faith gives readiness to believe what should be believed and discernment to reject what should not.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e323.summary: Reply to the first objection: an infused habit resembles an innate one, the natural habit given in creation, the infused in restoration. The natural habit of principles needs sense to determine its knowledge, while an acquired habit receives determination through the acts that produce it. Likewise faith must receive determination from our side. In this respect faith is said to be acquired through theology, which distinguishes the articles, as the habit of principles is acquired through sense as to their distinction but not as to the light by which they are known.
claims: Infused faith, like the innate habit of principles, needs external determination of its content.
Theology supplies the determination of the articles, not the light of faith itself.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e326.summary: Reply to the second objection: four things are considered in faith: what is to be believed, the reason determining the will to believe, the will commanding the intellect, and the intellect executing. So although the habit is infused, faith as to its determination and act is from four things in us. As to what is believed, it is from hearing, since the content is determined by God's inner speech or an external voice. As to the reason inducing the will, it is from seeing something that shows God speaks in the preacher. As to command, it is from the will. As to execution, the act is from the intellect.
claims: Although infused, faith depends on factors in us for its content, motive, command and execution.
Faith's content comes from hearing, its motive from signs that God speaks in the preacher, its command from the will and its execution from the intellect.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e329.summary: Reply to the third objection: properly speaking the philosophers did not believe God omnipotent but knew it, since they demonstrated it. If some believed it without demonstration, they did not believe it on God's word but from some sign from which they conjectured it.
claims: The philosophers knew God's omnipotence by demonstration rather than believing it, or conjectured it from signs.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e332.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: the infused habit of faith cannot go into act unless faith is determined, by God through revelation or by a human through teaching. The same is true of the habit of principles.
claims: The infused habit of faith requires revelation or teaching to determine its object before it can act.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e335.summary: Reply to the fifth objection: the perfection of divine works comes from God; any imperfection in them comes from the recipient.
claims: Imperfection in divine works comes from the recipient.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e339.summary: Reply to the sixth objection: in an act of sin there is not only the lack of a due circumstance but the positing of an undue one, so it is not merely imperfect but evil, and so is not said to be from God. In the act of unformed faith something due is lacking, but nothing undue is posited. So the act is imperfect, not evil, and the act is from God, though the defect is not.
claims: Sin posits something undue and is evil, while unformed faith only lacks something due and is merely imperfect.
The act of unformed faith is from God, though its defect is not.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e357.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 1 (is there unformed faith in demons?): faith sees in a mirror and an enigma (1 Corinthians 13), and such knowledge arises in us because we know through sense, which demons do not. So demons cannot have unformed faith.
claims: Faith's enigmatic character derives from sense-dependence, which demons lack.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e360.summary: Second objection: unformed faith is a gratuitous gift, but after their sin no gratuitous gift is infused into angels, and before it they had vision, not faith.
claims: Demons received no gratuitous gift after sinning and so lack unformed faith.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e363.summary: Third objection: the act of faith comes from the will, and no deliberate act of the demons is good (Book II, d. 7). Since the act of unformed faith is good, demons do not have it.
claims: Demons cannot perform the good, voluntary act of faith.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e366.summary: Sed contra: the demons believe and tremble (James 2:19).
claims: Scripture says demons believe.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e378.summary: Second sed contra: a gloss on Romans 1 says that unformed faith is that of demons.
claims: Demons have unformed faith.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e393.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 2 (does unformed faith remain in heretics?): heretics believe the Trinity and the Incarnation, which are above nature and cannot be believed without infused faith. So infused faith remains in them.
claims: Heretics' belief in supernatural articles shows infused faith remains.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e396.summary: Second objection: in the sciences, forgetting one item of knowledge leaves the habit as to the rest. Faith is the habit of the articles, so a heretic who disbelieves one article retains faith for the others.
claims: Like science, faith can remain partially when one article is rejected.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e399.summary: Third objection: unformed faith is the principle of servile fear, which exists in demons and heretics.
claims: Servile fear in heretics shows they have unformed faith.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e402.summary: Sed contra: every infused habit is expelled by a contrary act, and the heretic performs an act opposed to faith.
claims: A heretic's contrary act expels the habit of faith.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e406.summary: Second sed contra: otherwise the heretic would be at once faithful and unfaithful, which is impossible.
claims: One cannot be at once faithful and unfaithful.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e415.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 1: faith essentially involves assent to what one neither sees nor can reduce to what one sees, induced by a reason that suffices to determine assent though not to produce vision. That reason may be taken from something created, as when a sign induces belief about God or other things, or from uncreated truth itself, as when we believe what God has said through his ministers. Belief of the first kind compels the intellect, since nothing contrary appears; belief of the second kind does not compel but is inclined by the will. Demons have faith in the first way: from their natural knowledge and from miracles, which they discern far more subtly than we do as exceeding nature, they are compelled to believe things beyond their natural knowledge. They do not have it in the second way.
claims: Faith's motive may be a created sign, which compels assent, or uncreated truth, which inclines the will.
Demons have a compelled faith arising from natural knowledge and their keen perception of miracles, not faith resting on divine testimony through the will.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e418.summary: Reply to the first objection: though demons lack the obscurity that comes to us from sense, they have another obscurity, in that they cannot reach the vision of truth through supernatural knowledge, and so are compelled by signs to believe.
claims: Demons' obscurity lies in their lack of supernatural vision, not in dependence on sense.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e421.summary: Reply to the second objection: the faith in demons is not an infused habit but proceeds from natural knowledge.
claims: Demonic faith is natural, not infused.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e424.summary: Reply to the third objection: in demons the intellect is compelled to assent, so their faith does not wholly proceed from free will.
claims: Demonic belief is compelled rather than freely willed.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e434.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 2: infused faith helps in two ways, by making us believe what is to be believed and by making us refuse assent to what is not. The first a person can achieve by human estimation without an infused habit. The second, discerning inclination to this rather than that ('not believing every spirit'), comes only from the infused habit. Since the heretic lacks it, the habit of faith does not remain. If the heretic believes some articles, it is from human reason; were they inclined by the habit of faith, they would reject what is contrary to faith, as every habit resists what opposes it.
claims: Only infused faith gives the discernment to reject what is contrary to faith.
The heretic lacks this discernment, so the habit of faith does not remain in them.
A heretic's belief in some articles rests on human estimation, not infused faith.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e437.summary: Reply to the first objection: though heretics believe something above nature, they do not believe it through an infused habit directing them but through human estimation.
claims: Heretics' belief in supernatural truths rests on human estimation.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e440.summary: Reply to the second objection: the habit of science inclines to its objects in the manner of reason, so one who has it can be ignorant of some things belonging to it. The habit of faith, not resting on reason, inclines in the manner of nature, like the moral virtues and the habit of principles. So while it remains, one believes nothing against faith.
claims: Science inclines by way of reason and tolerates partial ignorance, while faith inclines by way of nature and cannot coexist with contrary belief.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e443.summary: Reply to the third objection: servile fear is caused in heretics, as in demons, by that human estimation.
claims: Servile fear in heretics arises from human estimation.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e461.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 1 (is unformed faith removed when charity comes?): 'when the perfect comes, what is partial will pass away' (1 Corinthians 13:10), as faith passes away when vision comes. Unformed faith is imperfect relative to formed, so it is removed when formed faith comes.
claims: The perfect removes the imperfect, so formed faith removes unformed faith.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e467.summary: Second objection: unformed faith is the principle of servile fear, which is removed when charity comes. So unformed faith is removed too.
claims: As servile fear passes with charity, so does unformed faith.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e470.summary: Third objection: grace is no less effective in a believer than in an unbeliever, in whom it causes the whole habit of faith. Since formed and unformed faith are of one species and two forms of one species cannot coexist in one subject, unformed faith must be removed when charity and grace come.
claims: Two forms of one species cannot coexist, so the new formed faith must replace the unformed.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e473.summary: Sed contra: infused gifts are more permanent than acquired ones, and grace does not remove acquired habits. So much less does it remove the infused habit of faith.
claims: Grace does not remove even acquired habits, still less infused faith.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e477.summary: Second sed contra: nothing is corrupted except by its contrary, and unformed faith is not contrary to grace, since good habits are not contrary to one another.
claims: Good habits are not contraries, so grace does not corrupt unformed faith.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e486.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 2 (does the act of unformed faith remain?): through unformed faith a good thing is done but not done well, while through formed faith it is done well. So the act of unformed faith does not remain.
claims: The act of unformed faith, not done well, gives way to the act of formed faith.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e489.summary: Second objection: a lesser light does not illuminate in the presence of a greater, and unformed faith is a lesser light than charity.
claims: The greater light of charity eclipses unformed faith's act.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e492.summary: Third objection: the virtuous person acts as well as possible, as nature does. The act of formed faith is better than that of unformed, so the latter lapses, as one who can demonstrate does not bother with dialectical syllogisms.
claims: One capable of the better act does not perform the lesser.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e495.summary: Sed contra: in moral matters, and especially with infused habits, nothing is in vain, and a habit without act would be in vain, since act is its end.
claims: A habit without its act would be pointless.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e499.summary: Second sed contra: the act of unformed faith is believing God or God's word, and this remains when charity comes.
claims: Believing God remains after charity arrives.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e508.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 3 (can unformed faith become formed?): unformed faith is dead (James 2), and a dead work is not revived, so unformed faith is not revived by charity.
claims: Dead faith, like a dead work, cannot be revived.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e511.summary: Second objection: faith is an accident, and accidents cannot change (Boethius). So the same faith that was unformed cannot become formed.
claims: As an accident, faith cannot itself undergo change from unformed to formed.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e514.summary: Third objection: two accidents do not make one, and grace is one accident. So grace does not form the prior unformed faith but causes a new habit of formed faith.
claims: Grace and faith cannot combine into one accident, so a new habit must be caused.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e517.summary: Sed contra: nature always works by the shortest way, and so does grace. It is shorter to form a pre-existing habit than to infuse a new one.
claims: Grace forms the existing faith rather than infusing a new one, as the shorter way.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e521.summary: Second sed contra: an infused habit is more akin to grace than a natural power, and grace forms imperfect natural powers. So much more does it form unformed faith.
claims: Grace, which perfects natural powers, all the more perfects unformed faith.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e531.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 1: removing what does not belong to a thing's species does not remove its substance, as air remains when darkness is removed. Unformedness does not belong to faith's species, which comes from its mode as determined by its subject power's relation to its object. Faith is called formed or unformed by relation to something extrinsic, the will, as air is lit by facing a luminous body. Since charity removes only unformedness, the substance of the habit of faith remains.
claims: Unformedness is not part of the species of faith, which is set by its power and object.
Formed and unformed are said of faith by relation to the will, something extrinsic.
When charity comes it removes only unformedness, and the habit of faith remains.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e534.summary: Reply to the first objection: faith's imperfection relative to vision is within the genus of cognition and so belongs to its species, which is why vision removes faith. That is not the case here.
claims: Vision removes faith because faith's imperfection relative to vision is specific, unlike its unformedness.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e537.summary: Reply to the second objection: servile fear also is not removed as a habit, only in its servility.
claims: Charity removes the servility of fear, not the fear itself.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e540.summary: Reply to the third objection: grace does not cause another habit of faith in one who already has it. This is not because grace is ineffective but because the subject cannot receive what it already has.
claims: Grace does not cause a second habit of faith because the subject already has one.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e549.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 2: as the habit of unformed faith remains without its unformedness, so does the act, since a habit is that by which one acts when the time comes (Augustine).
claims: The act of faith remains after charity comes, only without unformedness.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e555.summary: Reply to the first objection: doing good through unformed faith belongs to the substance of the habit and remains; not doing it well belongs to its unformedness and does not remain.
claims: The good of faith's act remains; only its deficiency in mode is removed.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e558.summary: Reply to the second objection: the light of unformed faith and charity are not of one ratio, so one does not obscure the other but perfects it, one being material relative to the other.
claims: Faith and charity are not competing lights; charity perfects faith as form perfects matter.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e561.summary: Reply to the third objection: the act of unformed faith falls short of formed faith only in its unformedness, and in that respect it does not remain.
claims: What lapses is only the unformedness of the act.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e570.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 3: as Aristotle notes in Ethics VI, before moral virtue is complete there is a natural inclination to it, called natural virtue, which becomes virtue in the full sense when reason perfects it. Similarly unformed faith pre-exists in the intellect before the complete being of virtue and takes on the ratio of virtue from the perfection of the higher power, the will. So one and the same faith, once unformed, becomes formed. No other faith comes, since formed and unformed faith do not differ in species, and two forms of one species cannot coexist, since forms are multiplied numerically only by diverse matter or subject.
claims: Unformed faith becomes formed faith in the same way natural virtue becomes full virtue when perfected by a higher power.
It is numerically the same faith, since two forms of one species cannot coexist in one subject.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e573.summary: Reply to the first objection: a dead work passes away and cannot be taken up again numerically, so it cannot be revived. But the unformed habit remains and can therefore be formed.
claims: A dead work passes, but an unformed habit persists and can be formed.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e576.summary: Reply to the second objection: an accident does not change as the subject of change, but the subject changes in its relation according to the accident, as in the intensification and remission of heat.
claims: Change in accidents is change of the subject according to the accident.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e579.summary: Reply to the third objection: grace and faith do not form one accident. Rather, charity's mode is participated for the perfection of faith, as prudence's mode is participated for the perfection of moral virtue. In this sense charity is said to form the pre-existing faith.
claims: Charity forms faith by communicating its mode, as prudence perfects moral virtue.

ta-l3d23q3-d1e589.summary: Exposition of Lombard's text. Aquinas distinguishes senses of 'faith' in the passage 'faith is taken in three ways'. Faith properly is assent to what one does not see, which arises either through human reason or through divine reason. Through human reason, faith means strong opinion; by extension, any certainty produced by human reasoning, even leading to sight (an 'argument' is a reason producing faith in a doubtful matter); a person's truthfulness, which causes others to believe (Cicero's 'faith is the foundation of justice', meaning fidelity); and the conscience by which one holds to that truthfulness (Romans 14:23, glossed as conscience). Through divine reason, faith means the habit by which one believes, formed or unformed, as well as its act, its object, the sacrament as cause and sign of faith, and by extension any certainty about divine things, even when seen. On Augustine's 'not as bodies', Aquinas explains that Augustine separates experiential knowledge of one's own faith from four kinds of vision: external sight, imagination retaining what was seen, imaginative construction of unseen things, and intellectual vision of things outside us. 'What is faith but to believe what you do not see?' defines the habit by its proper act.
claims: 'Faith' signifies, through human reason, strong opinion, any rational certainty, human truthfulness, or conscience.
Through divine reason, 'faith' signifies the habit (formed or unformed), its act, its object, the sacrament, and any certainty about divine things.
Augustine distinguishes experiential knowledge of one's own faith from sensory, imaginative and intellectual vision.
Augustine's 'to believe what you do not see' defines the habit through its proper act.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e120.summary: Arguments on the first quaestiuncula, whether charity forms faith. The objections note that charity is posterior to faith, that faith has its own species, and that faith is formed by grace. The sed contra cites charity's role in making faith meritorious and acceptable to God.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e142.summary: Arguments on the second quaestiuncula, whether unformed faith is a virtue. The objections appeal to Augustine on virtues in the wicked, to the difficulty of belief, and to unformed faith's opposition to unbelief. The sed contra calls it dead and liable to misuse.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e167.summary: Arguments on the third quaestiuncula, whether formed and unformed faith differ in species. The objections argue from difference in genus, from charity as form, and from different acts. The sed contra argues from their shared object and from charity's extrinsic relation to faith.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e190.summary: Solution to the first quaestiuncula. As first mover among the powers, the will impresses its form on the powers it moves and brings them to the end. So charity, which perfects the will, is a common form participated by all virtues in powers moved by the will, and the end that consummates them. Faith, in the intellect as moved by the will, is formed by charity in this way while keeping its specific form from its own power and object. Faith as such precedes charity, formed faith follows it, and grace forms faith through charity.
claims: Charity forms faith as a common, participated form and as its end, while faith keeps its specific form.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e208.summary: Solution to the second quaestiuncula. The act of a moved power is perfect only if both mover and moved are perfected by habits, so the act of believing requires charity in the will as well as faith in the intellect. Unformed faith, lacking a perfect act, is not a virtue. Augustine uses 'virtue' broadly, virtue requires the virtuous mode of acting, and a disposition to virtue can also oppose vice.
claims: Unformed faith is not a virtue because, without charity, the act of believing is not perfect.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e226.summary: Solution to the third quaestiuncula: acts can be considered by natural species, from their object, or by moral species. Formed and unformed faith are identical in natural species and differ in moral species only as perfect and imperfect within one species, like disposition and habit. Natural species comes from power and object, moral species from the moving power.
claims: Formed and unformed faith are one species, differing only as perfect and imperfect in the moral order.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e352.summary: Arguments on the first quaestiuncula, whether demons have unformed faith. The objections cite the sense-based enigma of faith, the absence of grace in fallen angels, and the badness of demons' deliberate acts. The sed contra cites James ('the demons believe and tremble') and a gloss on Romans.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e388.summary: Arguments on the second quaestiuncula, whether unformed faith remains in heretics. The objections cite heretics' belief in supernatural articles, the analogy of partial loss of science, and servile fear. The sed contra notes that contrary acts expel infused habits and that one cannot be faithful and unfaithful at once.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e410.summary: Solution to the first quaestiuncula. Faith's motive can be a created sign, which compels assent, or uncreated truth, which inclines the will. Demons have the first kind: their natural knowledge and keen discernment of miracles compel them to believe what exceeds their nature. Their faith is not infused, not free, and obscure only in lacking supernatural vision.
claims: Demons have a natural, compelled faith arising from signs, not infused faith resting on divine testimony.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e429.summary: Solution to the second quaestiuncula. Infused faith alone gives the discernment to reject what is contrary to faith. The heretic lacks it, so the habit of faith does not remain, and any articles they hold rest on human estimation. Unlike science, which inclines by way of reason and tolerates partial ignorance, faith inclines by way of nature and cannot coexist with contrary belief.
claims: Heretics retain no infused faith, since they lack its discernment, and they believe what they do by human estimation.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e456.summary: Arguments on the first quaestiuncula, whether unformed faith is removed when charity comes. The objections argue that the perfect expels the imperfect, that servile fear passes, and that two forms of one species cannot coexist. The sed contra argues from the permanence of infused gifts and the absence of contrariety among good habits.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e481.summary: Arguments on the second quaestiuncula, whether the act of unformed faith remains. The objections argue that the act is not done well, is eclipsed by the greater light, and lapses before the better act. The sed contra replies that a habit without act would be in vain and that believing God remains.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e503.summary: Arguments on the third quaestiuncula, whether unformed faith itself becomes formed. The objections invoke dead works, the immutability of accidents, and the impossibility of two accidents making one. The sed contra appeals to grace working by the shortest way and perfecting natural powers.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e526.summary: Solution to the first quaestiuncula. Unformedness is not part of faith's species, which comes from its power and object, but a relation to something extrinsic, the will. So charity removes only unformedness, and the habit remains. Vision removes faith because faith's imperfection relative to vision is specific. Charity removes the servility of fear, not the fear. Grace does not cause a second habit where one already exists.
claims: The habit of faith remains when charity comes; only its unformedness is removed.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e544.summary: Solution to the second quaestiuncula: the act of faith remains along with the habit, losing only its unformedness. Its goodness belongs to the habit's substance, faith and charity are not competing lights (charity perfects faith as form perfects matter), and only the deficiency of the act lapses.
claims: The act of faith persists under charity, now done well.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e565.summary: Solution to the third quaestiuncula. As natural virtue becomes full virtue when reason perfects it, unformed faith becomes formed when the will is perfected by charity, and it is numerically the same faith, since two forms of one species cannot coexist. The habit, unlike a dead work, persists and can be formed. Change in accidents is change of the subject, and charity forms faith by communicating its mode, as prudence perfects moral virtue.
claims: The same faith that was unformed becomes formed through charity.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e103.summary: Prooemium to the question on the formation of faith, which lists four articles: whether faith is formed by charity, whether unformed faith is God's gift, whether it is in demons, and whether it remains when charity comes.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e112.summary: Article 1 explains how charity forms faith. Aquinas builds a theory of ordered agency: the will, as first mover of the soul's powers, impresses a common form on the powers it moves and uses their acts for the last end. So charity, the will's perfection, is a participated common form and the end of all virtues in powers moved by the will. Faith keeps its specific form from its own object and power. Unformed faith is not a virtue, because the act of a moved power is perfect only when both mover and moved are perfected, and without charity the believer's will is not. Yet formed and unformed faith are one natural species, differing morally only as perfect and imperfect within that species.
claims: Charity forms faith as the participated common form and end imparted by the perfected will.
Unformed faith is not a virtue because it lacks a perfect act.
Formed and unformed faith are the same in natural species and differ only as perfect and imperfect.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e245.summary: Article 2 argues that unformed faith is an infused gift of God, not an acquired habit. Acquired habits arise when a higher power is naturally determined to what the lower lacks, but no power is naturally determined to what exceeds reason. So faith must be infused, making the intellect ready to believe and discerning against error. Faith's content must nonetheless be determined from outside, by revelation or teaching, as the habit of principles needs sense. That is the sense in which faith is 'acquired' by theology and 'comes from hearing'. Faith's act involves four factors in us: its content from hearing, its motive from signs that God speaks in the preacher, its command from the will, and its execution by the intellect. The philosophers knew God's omnipotence by demonstration rather than believing it. Unformed faith is imperfect but not evil, since it lacks something due without positing anything undue, so its act is from God.
claims: Faith, even unformed, is infused, since no power is naturally determined to what exceeds reason.
Infused faith needs its content determined by revelation or teaching, as the habit of principles depends on sense.
Unformed faith is imperfect, not evil, and its act is from God.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e344.summary: Article 3 extends the analysis of unformed faith to demons and heretics. Demons believe in a compelled way: their natural knowledge and their keen perception of miracles force assent to what exceeds their nature. This is not infused faith resting on divine testimony through the will. Heretics lose the infused habit altogether, since infused faith alone gives the discernment that rejects what is contrary to faith. Faith inclines by way of nature, not of reason, so it cannot coexist with denial of any article, and whatever heretics still hold rests on human estimation.
claims: Demons have a natural faith compelled by evidence of signs, not infused faith.
Heretics who reject any article retain no infused faith, because faith inclines by way of nature and excludes contrary belief.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e448.summary: Article 4 argues that when charity comes, unformed faith is not removed but formed. Unformedness lies outside faith's species, being a relation to the will, so charity removes only the unformedness while the habit and its act remain. The same act is now done well, and charity perfects faith as form perfects matter rather than eclipsing it. The same numerical faith becomes formed, as natural virtue becomes full virtue under reason, since two forms of one species cannot coexist in one subject. Vision, by contrast, does remove faith, because faith's imperfection relative to vision belongs to its species.
claims: Unformed faith remains, as habit and as act, when charity comes; only its unformedness is removed.
The same faith that was unformed becomes formed, by participation in charity's mode.

ta-l3d23q3-Dd1e584.summary: Exposition of Lombard's text. Aquinas distinguishes the senses of 'faith': through human reason (strong opinion, rational certainty, truthfulness or fidelity, conscience) and through divine reason (the habit, formed or unformed, its act, its object, the sacrament, and any certainty about divine things). He explains that Augustine distinguishes the experiential knowledge of one's own faith from sensory, imaginative and intellectual vision, and that Augustine defines the habit of faith through its act.
claims: 'Faith' is said in many senses, grounded either in human or in divine reason.
Knowledge of one's own faith is experiential and distinct from every kind of vision.

ta-l3d23q3.summary: The third question of Distinction 23 concerns the formation of faith by charity. Article 1 develops a theory of ordered agency in which the will, as first mover of the soul's powers, imparts a common form and end to the habits of the powers it moves. Charity, as the will's perfection, is the participated form of faith, while faith keeps its specific form from its object and power. Unformed faith is therefore not a virtue, since its act is imperfect, yet it is the same species as formed faith, differing only as imperfect from perfect. Article 2 shows that even unformed faith is infused, since nothing natural determines a power to what exceeds reason, though its content must be determined by revelation or teaching. Article 3 contrasts the compelled, natural faith of demons with infused faith and argues that heretics, by rejecting any article, lose the infused habit entirely. Article 4 holds that when charity comes, unformed faith is not removed but becomes formed, the same numerical habit and act perfected by charity. An expositio distinguishes the many senses of 'faith' in Lombard's text. The question establishes how a single habit of faith can exist dead or alive, and why its life comes from charity in the will.
claims: Charity forms faith as the common form and end imparted by the perfected will, while faith keeps its own specific form.
Unformed faith is an infused gift but not a virtue, being imperfect yet of the same species as formed faith.
Demons have a compelled natural faith, and heretics lose infused faith entirely.
When charity comes, the same faith that was unformed becomes formed.
